name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q01 - Count Rumford cannon boring experiment on heat

questiontext.text: In 1798, Benjamin Thomson (Count Rumford) performed experiments on the boring of brass cannons. Which of the following observations provided crucial evidence against the caloric theory of heat?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the caloric theory
The caloric theory treated heat as an invisible, weightless fluid that filled the pores of matter and flowed from hotter to colder bodies. According to this picture, boring a cannon with a sharper drill would scoop out more caloric fluid from the pores, producing more heat.

Step 2: Analyze Count Rumford's experimental findings
Rumford observed that the amount of heat produced during the boring of brass cannons depended directly on the mechanical work done (by the horses turning the drill) and continued indefinitely as long as work was supplied, without depending on the sharpness of the drill.

Step 3: Deduce the physical significance
Because heat could be generated continuously from mechanical work and did not depend on the sharpness of the drill, heat could not be a conserved fluid stored in pores. Instead, heat was recognized as a form of energy converted from mechanical work.

Final Answer:
Heat produced depended on the mechanical work done and not on the sharpness of the drill.

answer.text: The heat generated depended on the mechanical work done and not on the drill's sharpness.
A sharper drill scooped out significantly more caloric fluid from the brass.
The caloric fluid flowed spontaneously from colder regions to hotter regions of the cannon.
The cannon's mass decreased noticeably due to the loss of caloric fluid.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q02 - Distinction between mechanical and thermodynamic states

questiontext.text: A high-speed bullet is fired from a gun into a wooden block and comes to rest inside it. Regarding the mechanical and thermodynamic states of the bullet, which of the following statements is physically correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the nature of mechanical state
While the bullet is moving in flight, its motion is coordinated motion of the body as a whole, characterized by kinetic energy of its center of mass. Thermodynamics is not concerned with the motion of the system as a whole.

Step 2: Analyze the transition upon stopping
When the bullet pierces the wood and comes to rest, its bulk mechanical kinetic energy is dissipated into random, disordered molecular motion of the bullet and wood.

Step 3: Relate internal motion to temperature
Temperature is a measure of the internal disordered kinetic and potential energy of the molecules in the frame where the center of mass is at rest. Hence, the bullet's temperature rises only after its mechanical energy is converted into disordered internal thermal energy.

Final Answer:
The bullet's temperature rises when its bulk kinetic energy converts into disordered internal molecular motion upon stopping.

answer.text: The bullet's temperature is highest during flight because of its large bulk kinetic energy.
The temperature rises because the bulk mechanical kinetic energy transforms into disordered internal molecular motion.
Thermodynamics describes the motion of the center of mass of the bullet under external forces.
The temperature of the bullet decreases upon stopping because mechanical kinetic energy is conserved.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q03 - Definition of thermodynamic equilibrium of a system

questiontext.text: In thermodynamics, a macroscopic system is said to be in an equilibrium state when:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Contrast mechanics with thermodynamics
In mechanics, equilibrium means that the net external force and the net external torque acting on the system are zero.

Step 2: Formulate thermodynamic equilibrium
In thermodynamics, a system is in an equilibrium state when its macroscopic state variables—such as pressure, volume, temperature, mass, and chemical composition—do not change with time throughout the system.

Step 3: Evaluate microscopic behavior
Even though the macroscopic parameters remain strictly constant in time, the microscopic constituents (molecules) continue their incessant random motion.

Final Answer:
The macroscopic variables characterizing the system do not change with time.

answer.text: all microscopic molecular motions completely cease throughout the system.
only the net external mechanical force on the system is zero, regardless of temperature gradients.
the macroscopic state variables characterizing the system remain constant in time.
the volume of the system continuously increases while its temperature remains fixed.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q04 - Behavior of adiabatic and diathermic boundaries

questiontext.text: Two closed gaseous systems are placed in thermal contact. Which type of partition prevents any exchange of heat between them, and which type allows heat to flow until thermal equilibrium is established?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define an adiabatic boundary
An adiabatic wall is an insulating wall that does not allow the flow of heat energy between the separated systems.

Step 2: Define a diathermic boundary
A diathermic wall is a thermally conducting wall that permits heat energy to transfer freely between the systems until they equalize in temperature.

Step 3: Establish the equilibrium condition
Under a diathermic wall, heat flows spontaneously until the temperatures equalise, achieving thermal equilibrium.

Final Answer:
An adiabatic wall prevents heat exchange, whereas a diathermic wall permits heat transfer until thermal equilibrium is reached.

answer.text: A diathermic wall prevents heat flow; an adiabatic wall permits heat flow until equilibrium is attained.
Both adiabatic and diathermic walls completely prevent the flow of heat between systems.
Neither adiabatic nor diathermic walls allow systems to reach equal temperatures.
An adiabatic wall prevents heat flow; a diathermic wall permits heat flow until equilibrium is attained.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q05 - Zeroth law of thermodynamics formal statement

questiontext.text: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics, formulated by R. H. Fowler in 1931, states that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: State the experimental observation
If system A is in thermal equilibrium with system C, and system B is also separately in thermal equilibrium with system C, then when A and B are placed in thermal contact via a diathermic wall, no heat flows between them.

Step 2: Formalize the Zeroth Law
Two systems in thermal equilibrium with a third system separately are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

Step 3: Conclude the fundamental significance
This law defines temperature as a transitive thermodynamic state variable that takes the same value for systems in mutual thermal equilibrium.

Final Answer:
Two systems in thermal equilibrium with a third system separately are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

answer.text: two systems in thermal equilibrium with a third system separately are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
the total energy of an isolated thermodynamic system is strictly conserved in all processes.
heat cannot flow spontaneously from a cooler body to a warmer body without external work.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q06 - Physical concept introduced by Zeroth Law

questiontext.text: Which fundamental thermodynamic property is directly introduced and defined by the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the consequence of the Zeroth Law
The Zeroth Law implies that there must exist a scalar physical quantity that has the exact same value for all systems that are in mutual thermal equilibrium.

Step 2: Identify this thermodynamic property
This physical property, which serves as a marker of thermal equilibrium and determines the direction of heat flow, is temperature (\(T\)).

Step 3: Relate to other laws
The First Law introduces internal energy, and the Second Law introduces entropy. The Zeroth Law establishes temperature and the basis of thermometry.

Final Answer:
Temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q07 - Definition of internal energy of a gas

questiontext.text: In thermodynamics, the internal energy \(U\) of a gas contained in a vessel is best defined as the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reference frame definition
Internal energy is evaluated in the reference frame in which the center of mass of the system is at rest.

Step 2: Account for molecular energies
It is the sum of the molecular kinetic energies (associated with translational, rotational, and vibrational disordered motions) and the potential energies associated with intermolecular interactions.

Step 3: Exclude macroscopic motion
It explicitly excludes the overall macroscopic kinetic energy of the container as a whole or its macroscopic gravitational potential energy.

Final Answer:
Sum of the kinetic and potential energies of the constituent molecules in the reference frame where the center of mass is at rest.

answer.text: total kinetic energy of the container moving with velocity relative to the laboratory frame.
heat content stored inside the pores of the substance that can be fully scooped out.
sum of the disordered kinetic and potential energies of all constituent molecules in the rest frame of the center of mass.
work done by the gas during its expansion from absolute zero volume to its present volume.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q08 - Nature of heat and work in thermodynamics

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes heat and work from internal energy in thermodynamics?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define state variables
A state variable (like internal energy \(U\), pressure \(P\), volume \(V\), and temperature \(T\)) has a unique value for a given equilibrium state, independent of the path taken to reach that state.

Step 2: Characterize heat and work
Heat and work are modes of energy transfer across the system boundaries resulting in changes in internal energy. They exist only in transit and depend on the specific path followed.

Step 3: Analyze physical phrasing
Phrases like 'a gas contains a certain amount of internal energy' are physically meaningful, while phrases like 'a gas contains a certain amount of heat or work' are physically meaningless.

Final Answer:
Heat and work are modes of energy transfer in transit and are path-dependent, whereas internal energy is a state variable.

answer.text: Heat and work are intrinsic state variables stored within the system, whereas internal energy is path-dependent.
A thermodynamic system in a given equilibrium state contains a definite amount of work and heat.
Neither heat, work, nor internal energy depends on the thermodynamic path connecting two states.
Heat and work are path-dependent modes of energy transfer, whereas internal energy is a thermodynamic state variable.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q09 - Classification of intensive and extensive thermodynamic variables

questiontext.text: Consider a system in thermodynamic equilibrium. If the system is divided into two identical equal halves, which of the following groups contains only intensive variables (variables that remain unchanged in each half)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the definition of intensive variables
Intensive variables do not depend on the size or extent of the system. When an equilibrium system is divided into two equal halves, intensive variables retain their original value in each half.

Step 2: Recall the definition of extensive variables
Extensive variables are proportional to the size or mass of the system. Their values are halved when the system is partitioned into two equal halves.

Step 3: Classify given variables
Volume \(V\), total mass \(M\), and internal energy \(U\) are extensive variables because their values are halved. Pressure \(P\), temperature \(T\), and density \(\rho\) remain identical in each half, and therefore are intensive variables.

Final Answer:
Pressure, temperature, and density.

answer.text: Pressure, temperature, and density
Volume, mass, and internal energy
Internal energy, pressure, and volume
Mass, temperature, and total entropy

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q10 - Characteristics of an ideal quasi-static process

questiontext.text: A quasi-static process is an idealized thermodynamic process characterized by the fact that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand why non-equilibrium states occur
Rapid changes (such as sudden expansion into vacuum or large temperature gradients) produce non-equilibrium states where pressure and temperature are non-uniform.

Step 2: Define quasi-static conditions
A quasi-static process is carried out infinitely slowly so that the system remains in thermal and mechanical equilibrium with its surroundings at every intermediate stage.

Step 3: Evaluate parameter differences
At every stage of a quasi-static process, the difference between the system's pressure and the external pressure, as well as the difference between their temperatures, is infinitesimally small.

Final Answer:
The process proceeds infinitely slowly such that the system remains in equilibrium at every intermediate stage.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q11 - Mathematical statement of first law of thermodynamics

questiontext.text: In standard NCERT physics convention, let \(\Delta Q\) be the heat supplied to the system, \(\Delta W\) be the work done by the system, and \(\Delta U\) be the change in internal energy. The First Law of Thermodynamics is expressed as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the conservation principle
The First Law of Thermodynamics is the application of the law of conservation of energy to thermodynamic systems.

Step 2: Apply the standard sign convention
When heat \(\Delta Q\) is absorbed by the system, part of this energy increases the internal energy of the system by \(\Delta U\), and the remaining part is converted into work done by the system on the surroundings \(\Delta W\).

Step 3: Write the formula
The mathematical expression is \(\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W\), or equivalently \(\Delta U = \Delta Q - \Delta W\).

Final Answer:
\(\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W\)

answer.text: \(\Delta Q + \Delta U + \Delta W = 0\)
\(\Delta U = \Delta Q + \Delta W\)
\(\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W\)
\(\Delta W = \Delta Q + \Delta U\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q12 - Rate of increase of internal energy calculation

questiontext.text: An electric heater supplies heat to a thermodynamic system at a steady rate of \(100\text{ W}\). Simultaneously, the system performs mechanical work on its surroundings at a rate of \(75\text{ J/s}\). At what rate is the internal energy of the system increasing?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify given rates and units
Given data: Rate of heat supplied: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = 100\text{ W} = 100\text{ J/s} \) Rate of work done by system: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}W}{\mathrm{d}t} = 75\text{ J/s}\)

Step 2: Apply the rate form of the First Law of Thermodynamics
From the First Law: \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}t} + \frac{\mathrm{d}W}{\mathrm{d}t} \]

Step 3: Solve for the rate of change of internal energy
Rearranging gives: \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} - \frac{\mathrm{d}W}{\mathrm{d}t} = 100\text{ J/s} - 75\text{ J/s} = 25\text{ J/s} \]

Final Answer:
\(25\text{ J/s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q13 - Internal energy change during vaporization of water

questiontext.text: At standard atmospheric pressure (\(1.013 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}^2\)), \(1.0\text{ g}\) of liquid water at \(100^\circ\text{C}\) has a volume of \(1.0\text{ cm}^3\). When converted completely into steam at \(100^\circ\text{C}\), it occupies \(1671\text{ cm}^3\). Given the latent heat of vaporization of water is \(2256\text{ J/g}\), what is the change in internal energy \(\Delta U\) of the water?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify given quantities
Given: Mass: \(m = 1.0\text{ g}\) Latent heat: \(L = 2256\text{ J/g}\) Heat supplied: \(\Delta Q = m L = 1.0 \times 2256\text{ J} = 2256\text{ J}\) Pressure: \(P = 1.013 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}\) Initial volume: \(V_1 = 1.0\text{ cm}^3 = 1.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3\) Final volume: \(V_2 = 1671\text{ cm}^3 = 1671 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3\)

Step 2: Calculate external work done against atmospheric pressure
\[ \Delta W = P(V_2 - V_1) = 1.013 \times 10^5 \times (1671 - 1) \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3 \] \[ \Delta W = 1.013 \times 10^5 \times 1670 \times 10^{-6} = 1.013 \times 0.1670 \times 10^3 \approx 169.2\text{ J} \]

Step 3: Apply First Law of Thermodynamics to find internal energy change
\[ \Delta U = \Delta Q - \Delta W = 2256\text{ J} - 169.2\text{ J} = 2086.8\text{ J} \]

Final Answer:
\(2086.8\text{ J}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q14 - Precise definition of one standard calorie

questiontext.text: Because the specific heat capacity of water varies slightly with temperature, the standard international definition of one calorie specifies raising the temperature of \(1\text{ g}\) of water over which specific temperature interval?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the temperature dependence of specific heat of water
Experimental measurements show that the specific heat capacity of water varies slightly between \(0^\circ\text{C}\) and \(100^\circ\text{C}\), having a slight minimum near \(40^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 2: Recall the precise definition of calorie
To achieve a standardized definition, one calorie is precisely defined as the amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of \(1\text{ g}\) of water from \(14.5^\circ\text{C}\) to \(15.5^\circ\text{C}\) at standard atmospheric pressure.

Step 3: Relate to Joules
Over this interval, \(1\text{ cal} = 4.186\text{ J}\).

Final Answer:
From \(14.5^\circ\text{C}\) to \(15.5^\circ\text{C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q15 - Molar heat capacity of solids at room temperature

questiontext.text: According to the law of equipartition of energy, each atom in a three-dimensional solid is modeled as an oscillator vibrating in three dimensions. The theoretical molar specific heat capacity \(C\) of such a solid at ordinary room temperature is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine the average energy per atom
In a solid of \(N\) atoms, each atom behaves as a harmonic oscillator in three dimensions. An oscillator in 1D has average kinetic energy \(\frac{1}{2}k_B T\) and average potential energy \(\frac{1}{2}k_B T\), giving total average energy \(k_B T\). In three dimensions, the average energy per atom is \(3 k_B T\).

Step 2: Compute total internal energy for one mole
For one mole of solid containing Avogadro's number \(N_A\) of atoms: \[ U = 3 N_A k_B T = 3 R T \]

Step 3: Differentiate to find molar specific heat capacity
Since thermal expansion is negligible for solids (\(P\Delta V \approx 0\)): \[ C = \frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}T} = 3R \]

Final Answer:
\(3R\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q16 - Molar heat capacities relation Mayer relation

questiontext.text: For an ideal gas, the molar specific heat capacity at constant pressure \(C_p\) is always greater than the molar specific heat capacity at constant volume \(C_v\) by the universal gas constant \(R\) (\(C_p - C_v = R\)). The fundamental physical reason for this difference is that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze heat absorption at constant volume
At constant volume (\(\Delta V = 0\)), the gas performs zero external work. Therefore, all heat supplied goes entirely into increasing the internal energy and raising the temperature: \(\Delta Q_v = \Delta U = C_v \Delta T\).

Step 2: Analyze heat absorption at constant pressure
At constant pressure, as the temperature rises, the gas must expand to keep pressure constant. Thus, the heat supplied must not only increase the internal energy by \(\Delta U\), but also do work against external pressure: \(\Delta Q_p = \Delta U + P\Delta V = C_p \Delta T\).

Step 3: Connect to the ideal gas law
For one mole of an ideal gas, \(P\Delta V = R\Delta T\). Hence \(C_p \Delta T = C_v \\Delta T + R\Delta T\), yielding \(C_p - C_v = R\). Additional heat is required to perform expansion work against external pressure.

Final Answer:
At constant pressure, additional heat must be supplied to do work in expanding against the external pressure while raising the temperature.

answer.text: the molecules of the gas lose internal kinetic energy when heated at constant pressure.
at constant volume, the gas does mechanical work on the rigid walls of the container.
the intermolecular forces of attraction increase dramatically at constant pressure.
at constant pressure, extra heat is needed to perform external work during expansion while raising the temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q17 - Work done in isothermal expansion of ideal gas

questiontext.text: Two moles of an ideal gas undergo a quasi-static isothermal expansion at temperature \(T = 300\text{ K}\) from an initial volume \(V_1 = 2\text{ L}\) to a final volume \(V_2 = 4\text{ L}\). Taking \(R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and \(\ln 2 = 0.693\), the work done by the gas during this expansion is closest to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify given parameters
Number of moles: \(\mu = 2\text{ mol}\) Temperature: \(T = 300\text{ K}\) Initial volume: \(V_1 = 2\text{ L}\) Final volume: \(V_2 = 4\text{ L}\) Volume ratio: \(\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{4}{2} = 2\) Universal gas constant: \(R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) Natural logarithm: \(\ln 2 = 0.693\)

Step 2: Apply the work formula for isothermal expansion
\[ W = \mu R T \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right) \]

Step 3: Substitute the numerical values and compute
\[ W = 2 \times 8.31 \times 300 \times \ln(2) \] \[ W = 4986 \times 0.693 = 3455.3\text{ J} \approx 3455\text{ J} \]

Final Answer:
\(3455\text{ J}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q18 - Internal energy change during isothermal process

questiontext.text: During a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, which of the following relationships correctly describes the change in internal energy \(\Delta U\) and the heat supplied \(Q\) to the gas?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand internal energy of an ideal gas
For an ideal gas, intermolecular potential energies are neglected. Therefore, the internal energy \(U\) depends solely on temperature \(T\).

Step 2: Evaluate \(\Delta U\) in an isothermal process
Since temperature remains constant throughout an isothermal process (\(\Delta T = 0\)), the change in internal energy is strictly zero: \(\Delta U = 0\).

Step 3: Apply First Law of Thermodynamics
From \(\Delta Q = \Delta U + W\), substituting \(\Delta U = 0\) yields \(Q = W\). All heat absorbed by the gas is converted completely into work done by the gas on the environment.

Final Answer:
\(\Delta U = 0\) and \(Q = W\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q19 - Adiabatic relation connecting temperature and volume

questiontext.text: An ideal gas with adiabatic exponent \(\gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v}\) undergoes a quasi-static adiabatic process. The relationship between its temperature \(T\) and volume \(V\) during this process is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the standard adiabatic relation
The pressure-volume relation for an adiabatic process of an ideal gas is: \[ P V^\gamma = \text{constant} \]

Step 2: Express pressure in terms of temperature and volume
From the ideal gas equation of state: \[ P V = \mu R T \implies P = \frac{\mu R T}{V} \]

Step 3: Substitute and simplify
Substituting \(P\) into the adiabatic equation: \[ \left(\frac{\mu R T}{V}\right) V^\gamma = \text{constant} \implies T V^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant} \]

Final Answer:
\(T V^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant}\)

\(T^\gamma V = \text{constant}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q20 - Work done in adiabatic expansion of ideal gas

questiontext.text: One mole of an ideal monoatomic gas (\(\gamma = \frac{5}{3}\)) expands adiabatically such that its temperature falls from \(400\text{ K}\) to \(300\text{ K}\). Taking \(R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), the work done by the gas is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify given parameters
Number of moles: \(\mu = 1\text{ mol}\) Initial temperature: \(T_1 = 400\text{ K}\) Final temperature: \(T_2 = 300\text{ K}\) Adiabatic exponent: \(\gamma = \frac{5}{3}\) Universal gas constant: \(R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Apply the work formula for an adiabatic process
The work done by an ideal gas in an adiabatic change is: \[ W = \frac{\mu R (T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1} \]

Step 3: Substitute values and calculate
Denominator: \[ \gamma - 1 = \frac{5}{3} - 1 = \frac{2}{3} \] Numerator: \[ \mu R (T_1 - T_2) = 1 \\times 8.31 \times (400 - 300) = 831\text{ J} \] Work done: \[ W = \frac{831}{\frac{2}{3}} = \frac{831 \times 3}{2} = \frac{2493}{2} = 1246.5\text{ J} \]

Final Answer:
\(1246.5\text{ J}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q21 - Comparison of isothermal and adiabatic curve slopes

questiontext.text: At a given common point \((P, V)\) on an indicator (\(P\)-\(V\)) diagram, how does the slope \(\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}V}\right)\) of an adiabatic curve compare with the slope of an isothermal curve for an ideal gas with ratio of specific heats \(\gamma > 1\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Compute the slope of an isothermal curve
For an isothermal process, \(P V = \text{constant}\). Differentiating with respect to \(V\): \[ P + V\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}V} = 0 \implies \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}V}\right)_{\text{iso}} = -\frac{P}{V} \]

Step 2: Compute the slope of an adiabatic curve
For an adiabatic process, \(P V^\gamma = \text{constant}\). Differentiating with respect to \(V\): \[ V^\gamma \frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}V} + \gamma P V^{\gamma - 1} = 0 \implies \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}V}\right)_{\text{ad}} = -\gamma \frac{P}{V} \]

Step 3: Compare both slopes
Comparing the two slopes: \[ \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}V}\right)_{\text{ad}} = \gamma \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}V}\right)_{\text{iso}} \] Since \(\gamma > 1\), the adiabatic curve is \(\gamma\) times steeper than the isothermal curve.

Final Answer:
The adiabatic curve is \(\gamma\) times steeper than the isothermal curve.

answer.text: The slope of the adiabatic curve is \(\gamma\) times the slope of the isothermal curve.
The slope of the isothermal curve is \(\gamma\) times the slope of the adiabatic curve.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q22 - Heat exchange during an isochoric process

questiontext.text: In an isochoric process involving an ideal gas, the volume remains constant throughout. Which of the following statements is strictly correct regarding the work done and heat absorbed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate work done
Mechanical work is defined as \(W = \int P \,\mathrm{d}V\). Since volume is constant (\(\mathrm{d}V = 0\)), no boundary displacement occurs, and \(W = 0\).

Step 2: Apply the First Law of Thermodynamics
Using \(\Delta Q = \Delta U + W\), when \(W = 0\), we obtain \(\Delta Q = \Delta U\).

Step 3: Conclude the temperature change
All heat added to the system goes entirely into increasing its internal energy and raising its temperature, governed by \(\Delta Q = \mu C_v \Delta T\).

Final Answer:
Work done is zero, and all heat absorbed goes entirely to increase internal energy.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q23 - Fraction of heat converted to isobaric work

questiontext.text: An ideal monoatomic gas (\(\gamma = \frac{5}{3}\)) is heated at constant pressure. What fraction of the total heat supplied to the gas is converted into work done by the gas in expanding?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Express heat supplied at constant pressure
For \(\mu\) moles of an ideal gas at constant pressure: \[ \Delta Q = \mu C_p \Delta T \]

Step 2: Express work done during isobaric expansion
At constant pressure: \[ \Delta W = P \Delta V = \mu R \Delta T \]

Step 3: Determine the ratio of work to heat

Final Answer:
The net change in internal energy is zero, and net heat absorbed equals net work done.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q35 - Work done calculation along alternative thermodynamic path

questiontext.text: In taking a gas adiabatically from an equilibrium state \(A\) to another equilibrium state \(B\), an amount of work equal to \(22.3\text{ J}\) is done on the system. If the gas is instead taken from state \(A\) to state \(B\) via an alternative process in which the net heat absorbed by the system is \(9.35\text{ cal}\), how much net work is done by the system in this second process? (Take \(1\text{ cal} = 4.19\text{ J}\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the adiabatic path from A to B
For the adiabatic process, \(Q_{\text{ad}} = 0\). Work done ON the system is \(22.3\text{ J}\), so work done BY the system is \(W_{\text{ad}} = -22.3\text{ J}\). From the First Law: \[ \Delta U = U_B - U_A = Q_{\text{ad}} - W_{\text{ad}} = 0 - (-22.3\text{ J}) = +22.3\text{ J} \]

Step 2: Understand the path independence of internal energy
Because internal energy is a state variable, the change in internal energy \(\Delta U = U_B - U_A = +22.3\text{ J}\) is identical for any process connecting state \(A\) to state \(B\).

Step 3: Apply the First Law to the second process
Heat absorbed in the second path: \[ Q_2 = 9.35\text{ cal} \times 4.19\text{ J/cal} = 39.1765\text{ J} \approx 39.18\text{ J} \] From \(\Delta U = Q_2 - W_2\): \[ W_2 = Q_2 - \Delta U = 39.18\text{ J} - 22.3\text{ J} = 16.88\text{ J} \approx 16.9\text{ J} \]

Final Answer:

Volume rate: \(3.0\text{ L/min} = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3\text{/min}\) Mass rate of water: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}m_w}{\mathrm{d}t} = 3.0\text{ kg/min} = 3000\text{ g/min}\) Temperature rise: \(\Delta T = 77^\circ\text{C} - 27^\circ\text{C} = 50^\circ\text{C} = 50\text{ K}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q37 - Work done along piecewise linear PV paths

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q40 - Carnot cycle adiabatic volume ratio proof

Starting from \(P V^\gamma = \text{constant}\) and \(V = \frac{\mu R T}{P}\): \[ P \left(\frac{T}{P}\right)^\gamma = \text{constant} \implies P^{1 - \gamma} T^\gamma = \text{constant} \] Equivalently: \[ T \propto P^{\frac{\gamma - 1}{\gamma}} \]

Step 2: Calculate the exponent for a monoatomic gas
For \(\gamma = \frac{5}{3}\): \[ \frac{\gamma - 1}{\gamma} = \frac{\frac{5}{3} - 1}{\frac{5}{3}} = \frac{\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{5}{3}} = \frac{2}{5} = 0.4 \]

Step 3: Calculate the final temperature
Given \(\frac{P_2}{P_1} = 32\): \[ \frac{T_2}{T_1} = (32)^{2/5} = \left(2^5\right)^{2/5} = 2^2 = 4 \] Therefore: \[ T_2 = 4 \times T_1 = 4 \times 300\text{ K} = 1200\text{ K} \]

Final Answer:
\(1200\text{ K}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q43 - Coefficient of performance of a Carnot refrigerator

questiontext.text: A Carnot refrigerator operates between a cold compartment at \(-3^\circ\text{C}\) and surroundings at \(27^\circ\text{C}\). Its coefficient of performance \(\alpha\), and the mechanical work required to remove \(1800\text{ J}\) of heat from the cold compartment, are respectively:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Convert temperatures to Kelvin
Cold compartment: \(T_2 = -3 + 273 = 270\text{ K}\) Surroundings: \(T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}\)

Step 2: Calculate coefficient of performance \(\alpha\)
For a Carnot refrigerator: \[ \alpha = \frac{Q_2}{W} = \frac{T_2}{T_1 - T_2} = \frac{270}{300 - 270} = \frac{270}{30} = 9 \]

Step 3: Calculate the required work
Given heat removed \(Q_2 = 1800\text{ J}\): \[ W = \frac{Q_2}{\alpha} = \frac{1800\text{ J}}{9} = 200\text{ J} \]

Final Answer:
\(\alpha = 9\) and \(W = 200\text{ J}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q44 - Microscopic interpretation of latent heat of vaporization

questiontext.text: When \(1\text{ g}\) of water at \(100^\circ\text{C}\) boils into steam at atmospheric pressure, \(2256\text{ J}\) of heat is absorbed, of which \(169.2\text{ J}\) is spent in external work against atmospheric pressure and \(2086.8\text{ J}\) increases internal energy. At the molecular level, what accounts for this large increase in internal energy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the change in molecular kinetic energy
Because the phase transition occurs at constant temperature (\(100^\circ\text{C}\)), the average disordered translational kinetic energy of the water molecules does not change.

Step 2: Examine the change in molecular potential energy
In the liquid state, water molecules are closely bound by strong attractive intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds and van der Waals interactions). Transitioning to vapor increases the average intermolecular separation by more than an order of magnitude.

Step 3: Account for the internal energy change
The vast majority of the heat absorbed (\(2086.8\text{ J}\), over \(92\%\)) is converted into intermolecular potential energy required to overcome and break these attractive forces against mutual cohesion.

Final Answer:
Work done against attractive intermolecular forces to separate water molecules into vapor.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q45 - Intermediate non equilibrium states in free expansion

questiontext.text: Two thermally insulated cylinders \(A\) and \(B\) of equal capacity are connected via a stopcock. Cylinder \(A\) contains an ideal gas at pressure \(P\) and temperature \(T\), while \(B\) is evacuated. When the stopcock is suddenly opened, which of the following is true regarding the intermediate states before the system reaches final equilibrium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the nature of intermediate states during rapid expansion
During the rapid, turbulent rush of gas into cylinder \(B\), pressure, temperature, and density gradients exist throughout the volume. The system is violently out of thermodynamic equilibrium.

Step 2: Evaluate the concept of thermodynamic state variables
Thermodynamic state variables (such as uniform \(P\) and \(T\)) are well-defined only for equilibrium states. In non-equilibrium states, a single pressure or temperature cannot characterize the entire system.

Step 3: Determine whether intermediate states lie on the P-V-T surface
Because intermediate states are non-equilibrium states, they cannot be represented by a unique set of coordinates \((P, V, T)\) and therefore do NOT lie on the equilibrium \(P\)-\(V\)-\(T\) equation of state surface.

Final Answer:
The intermediate states are non-equilibrium states and do not lie on the equilibrium P-V-T surface.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q46 - Breakdown of Dulong Petit law at low temperatures

questiontext.text: The Dulong-Petit law predicts a constant molar specific heat capacity \(C = 3R\) for solids using classical equipartition of energy. At very low temperatures approaching absolute zero, experimental observations show that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the classical equipartition prediction
Classical equipartition treats atomic vibrations as continuous harmonic oscillators, yielding average energy \(3 k_B T\) per atom and hence a temperature-independent molar heat capacity \(C = 3R\).

Step 2: Examine experimental behavior at low temperatures
Experiments demonstrate that as temperature drops toward absolute zero (\(T \to 0\text{ K}\)), the molar heat capacity of all solids decreases sharply and approaches zero (varying as \(T^3\) for non-magnetic insulators).

Step 3: Identify the underlying physical reason
At low temperatures, thermal energy \(k_B T\) becomes smaller than the quantum vibrational energy levels (\(\hbar \omega\)), 'freezing out' vibrational modes because classical continuous excitation is no longer possible.

Final Answer:
The molar specific heat decreases sharply and approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero.

Step 3: Evaluate operational advantages
A small temperature rise prevents the coolant from reaching excessive temperatures or boiling violently, while carrying away maximum heat per unit mass pumped.

It can absorb large amounts of heat with only a small rise in temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q48 - Net work done in cyclic triangular PV diagram

questiontext.text: An ideal gas undergoes a closed cyclic process \(A \to B \to C \to A\) in a clockwise direction on a \(P\)-\(V\) diagram. Step \(A \to B\) is an isobaric expansion at pressure \(P_1 = 4.0 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}^2\) from \(V_1 = 1.0\text{ m}^3\) to \(V_2 = 3.0\text{ m}^3\). Step \(B \to C\) is an isochoric depressurization to pressure \(P_2 = 1.0 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}^2\). Step \(C \to A\) is a linear compression directly back to state \(A\). The net work done by the gas in one complete cycle is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: State the graphical interpretation of work in a cyclic process
The net work done per cycle equals the area enclosed by the closed loop on a \(P\)-\(V\) diagram. A clockwise cycle encloses positive net work, while a counterclockwise cycle represents negative work.

Step 2: Identify the geometry of the enclosed cycle
The path forms a right-angled triangle \(A B C\) with vertices at \(A(1.0, 4.0 \times 10^5)\), \(B(3.0, 4.0 \times 10^5)\), and \(C(3.0, 1.0 \times 10^5)\). Base of the triangle: \(b = V_2 - V_1 = 3.0 - 1.0 = 2.0\text{ m}^3\) Height of the triangle: \(h = P_1 - P_2 = (4.0 - 1.0) \times 10^5 = 3.0 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}^2\)

Step 3: Compute the area and net work
\[ W_{\text{net}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times (2.0\text{ m}^3) \times (3.0 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}^2) = 3.0 \times 10^5\text{ J} \] Since the cycle is traced clockwise, \(W_{\text{net}} = +3.0 \times 10^5\text{ J}\).

Final Answer:
\(+3.0 \times 10^5\text{ J}\)
